content.authoring_prompt: Analyze the consequences of violating the 1:1 constraint that requires one stateful session per server. Identify which session-scoped guarantees break — protocol negotiation and capability exchange, bidirectional message routing, subscription/notification management, and per-server security isolation — and explain how each fails. Describe concrete interoperability and security impacts, including how host-enforced security/consent boundaries can be compromised. Propose specific mitigations or design changes to restore isolation, correct routing and subscription semantics, and preserve capability scoping.
content.suggested_opener: During a rollout, a proxy multiplexes sessions violating one stateful session per server

content.authoring_prompt: List the specific host-enforced controls required so servers cannot read the whole conversation or see into other servers. Include: keeping the full conversation history local; providing only the minimal contextual information each server needs; maintaining isolated per-server connections; and mediating or blocking cross-server interactions. For each control briefly state how the host enforces it. Conclude with the security implications if any control is violated (how servers could read the entire conversation or access other servers' data, breaking isolation and exposing sensitive context).
content.suggested_opener: Your host accidentally transmits full conversation history to a per-server connection.

content.authoring_prompt: Design an implementation that defends a host against undeclared UI features and mid-session capability changes. Describe how you will enforce predeclared templates, render HTML only in sandboxed iframes, use auditable MCP JSON-RPC messages for UI-to-host communication, require explicit user consent for UI-initiated calls, and provide text-only fallbacks. Provide concrete APIs and message flows, error handling for unrenderable or failed UI/tool calls, and required audit/logging. Explain how the design preserves backward compatibility and enables gradual host adoption.
content.suggested_opener: During a feature rollout, a server begins sending undeclared UI templates to hosts.

content.authoring_prompt: Identify what breaks in the protocol if a request ID previously used within the same session is reused. Reference the requirement that requests MUST include a string or integer ID, that the ID MUST NOT be null, and that the request ID MUST NOT have been previously used by the requestor within the same session. Describe what implementations must do to prevent or detect reuse and ensure each request supplies a non-null string or integer ID unique per requestor within a session. Keep answers concise and grounded only in those requirements.
content.suggested_opener: During a session, the client sends duplicate string or integer request IDs.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain why all MCP implementations MUST support the Base Protocol and Lifecycle Management. Analyze how core JSON-RPC message types, connection initialization, capability negotiation, and session control form the minimal interoperable core. Describe the architectural implications for server and client design, including required lifecycle behaviors and a modular separation-of-concerns that allows optional components to be added or omitted. Give one concrete example of a mandatory behavior and one example of integrating an optional component cleanly.
content.suggested_opener: During design review, a colleague questions requiring JSON-RPC and lifecycle management.

content.authoring_prompt: Give the candidate one or more MCP/JSON-RPC response examples and ask them to evaluate compliance. Require verification that each response includes the same ID as its request and sets exactly one of `result` or `error`. If the response uses `error`, require the error object to include an integer `code` and a `message`. Have the candidate enumerate which failure mode(s) are present (both set, none set, non-integer code, mismatched/unknown ID) and describe minimal corrective changes.
content.suggested_opener: A production incident occurs when MCP/JSON-RPC responses include non-integer error codes.

content.authoring_prompt: Ask the candidate to design an implementation for an MCP receiver that uses STDIO transport and may lack an authorization context. Describe how credentials and access control become host-local concerns and when the receiver must bind tasks to an authorization context. Specify concrete safeguards: generate cryptographically secure task IDs with sufficient entropy, use shorter TTLs when context-binding is unavailable, reject tasks/get, tasks/result, and tasks/cancel requests across contexts, and ensure tasks/list returns only the requestors tasks. Include rate limiting and documentation practices to mitigate enumeration and DoS risks.
content.suggested_opener: A production service uses STDIO transport and provides no authorization context.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze the architectural trade-offs and responsibilities of splitting MCP into server roles that expose capability surfaces (Resources, Tools, Prompts) and client roles that orchestrate the LLM interaction and invoke those server-exposed tools. Explain how that split affects reuse, operational complexity, deployment, scaling, and security boundaries, explicitly referencing the “What’s happening under the hood” sequence. Recommend where to deploy servers so they can securely run tool logic and data access, how clients should reliably discover and launch those servers (respecting transport-specific constraints), and how to treat the server as the execution/logging boundary. Justify your recommendations with concrete trade-offs and operational mitigations.
content.suggested_opener: During an incident, client fails to discover MCP server exposing Tools and Resources.

content.authoring_prompt: Ask the candidate to produce a concrete implementation plan enforcing MCP requirements: robust authorization, explicit user consent flows, and strict token management for agents or servers acting on users’ behalf. Require detailed designs for scoped tokens, consent UX, revocation mechanisms, and auditability, showing stepwise flows and API behavior for each control. Have them explain how each proposed mechanism limits model access and protects user data in line with the "Understanding Authorization in MCP" guidance.
content.suggested_opener: Your team is designing scoped tokens and consent UX for agents acting on users' behalf

content.authoring_prompt: Produce an implementation plan to harden a server+client pipeline that integrates heterogeneous tools. Enumerate concrete server-side measures: validate all tool inputs, implement proper access controls, rate limit tool invocations, sanitize tool outputs, and publish/enforce input/output schemas. Enumerate concrete client-side measures: prompt for user confirmation on sensitive operations, show tool inputs before calls, validate tool results before passing to the LLM, enforce timeouts, and log tool usage. Provide brief API-contract examples, error-handling flows that surface tool execution errors, and one checklist to prevent data exfiltration.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you find unchecked Google Calendar API inputs and annotations.

content.authoring_prompt: Design a concrete MCP tool specification for a state‑modifying operation (for example, a 3D printer job submission) that implements the listed mitigations. Provide a clear name and description, explicit side‑effect annotations (readOnly/destructive/idempotent/openWorld), detailed JSON Schema for parameters with examples, and sample invocations. Specify human‑in‑the‑loop confirmation flows, progress/status reporting format, focused/atomic operation boundaries, expected return value structures, and robust error handling with validation and cleanup guidance. Include operational controls: timeouts, rate limiting, access control, and audit/logging primitives, plus expected logs and recovery steps.
content.suggested_opener: During deployment, a model invokes a destructive, non‑idempotent tool on production

content.authoring_prompt: Require the candidate to implement host and client behavior for MCP JSON-RPC resource methods (resources/list, resources/read, resources/subscribe). They must present pseudocode or sequence diagrams that validate resource URIs, enforce access controls and permissions, properly encode/handle text and base64-encoded binary payloads, and emit listChanged and subscribe notifications. Ask for explicit JSON-RPC error responses for resource-not-found (-32002), internal errors (-32603), malformed or improperly encoded payloads, and permission/authorization failures. Request a set of unit tests or test scenarios that exercise these runtime failure modes and demonstrate correct JSON-RPC error objects.
content.suggested_opener: A host must implement resources/read and return -32002 for missing URIs.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain what is meant by the sentence: "MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems." State three concise, high-level implications that follow directly from that sentence for engineers integrating MCP. Do not assume any MCP features or responsibilities beyond this quoted description. Keep each implication to one short sentence and base answers only on the provided quote.
content.suggested_opener: During planning, you assess MCP for connecting AI applications to external systems.

content.authoring_prompt: You are designing host-side controls for an MCP Client that will host server-provided UI. Produce a concise implementation plan mapping MCP Client features to concrete controls. Specify how to use the MCP Roots capability, the Prompt System for declared templates, and client-side sampling/elicitation handlers to gate model calls and data access. Describe routing UI↔host traffic over the message transport/JSON-RPC, using transport request customizers and McpTransportContext to bind requests to authenticated sessions and tightly control HTTP headers, and registering loggingConsumer and setLoggingLevel for auditable logs. For each control include the MCP Client API calls or configuration, expected behavior, and failure modes.
content.suggested_opener: During deployment, MCP Client requests lacked McpTransportContext-bound authenticated session headers.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain the constraints of supporting only text/html rendered in sandboxed iframes. List which content types are explicitly deferred: external URLs, remote DOM, and native widgets. Describe concrete, actionable steps servers and tool designers must take to remain compatible and avoid degraded UX (for example: produce self-contained text/html responses; ensure renderability inside sandboxed iframes; preserve screenshot/preview capabilities). Briefly state how this approach provides universal browser support, a well-understood security model, and a baseline for future extensions.
content.suggested_opener: Your integration must return self-contained text/html that renders in sandboxed iframes

content.authoring_prompt: Design how servers and hosts should behave when a host cannot or refuses to render ui:// resources. Specify host detection logic for when to switch to the server’s text-based flow and how to avoid partial UI execution. Describe the server-side strategy to always return a text-only fallback and structured, meaningful non-UI content (include a sample response schema). Show brief pseudocode or HTTP examples for both sides, and explain how this preserves tool functionality while supporting MCP Apps’ optional, gradual UI adoption.
content.suggested_opener: During integration, hosts cannot render ui:// templates and require text-only fallback.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze the quoted API Base URL listing (Production, Staging, Local, Custom). Explain why this listing alone is insufficient to prescribe safe mid-session host switching and how that could lead to mixing discovery results, session state, request IDs, or message ordering. Specify the exact additional documentation topics required (for example: session boundaries, cache/ID invalidation, re-discovery procedures) and justify why each is necessary. Conclude with a single recommended next step for the documentation team.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, API Base URL lists Production, Staging, Local, Custom.

content.authoring_prompt: Decide whether to use registry-listed public MCP servers or a custom/self-hosted MCP for a production service. State your choice and justify it by explicitly referencing control tradeoffs: authentication, access control, data handling, tooling, and SLAs. List the responsibilities self-hosting shifts to the integrator: designing/operating (scaling, monitoring, backup), capability discovery and schema/version compatibility, enforcing authz and tenant isolation, sandboxing/vetting tools and resources, and compliance and upgrade procedures. For each responsibility, briefly describe how you would satisfy it while preserving SLAs.
content.suggested_opener: Your team must evaluate authentication, access control, SLAs for registry or self-hosted MCP.

content.authoring_prompt: Ask the candidate to produce a concrete implementation plan. First, explain what breaks and why reuse of a request ID within the same MCP session makes the session non-compliant. Then specify exactly how an MCP implementation should generate, validate, and enforce request IDs consistent with the documented requirements: requests MUST include a string or integer ID, the ID MUST NOT be `null`, and the request ID MUST NOT have been previously used by the requestor within the same session. Include the runtime checks, the per-requestor session state to track, and the enforcement behavior when reuse is detected.
content.suggested_opener: A production incident occurs when a requestor reuses a request ID in session

content.authoring_prompt: You maintain an MCP client and server. Implement two authentication paths: one for HTTP-based transport that conforms to the MCP Authorization specification, and one for STDIO transport that retrieves credentials from the environment. Add a configurable negotiation hook allowing clients and servers to negotiate custom authentication and authorization strategies. Provide code sketches or configuration plus tests demonstrating the correct credential source per transport and a brief note about whether the specification lists security implications for deviating.
content.suggested_opener: During integration, ensure HTTP-based transport conforms; STDIO retrieves credentials from the environment.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain how an MCP server must implement receiving JSON-RPC batches. Describe parsing an incoming JSON array that contains multiple requests and/or notifications, and how the server should accept and process array-encoded batches even if it never sends batches itself. Call out required behaviors (MUST support receiving) versus optional behaviors (MAY support sending), and enumerate error-handling and validation decisions for malformed arrays or mixed request/notification entries.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review you find MCP implementations ignoring array-encoded JSON-RPC batches.

content.authoring_prompt: Create a short-answer exam item that verifies precise comprehension of the MCP mandatory response validation rules. Require the candidate to enumerate the mandatory rules exactly: responses must include the same ID as the request; either a result or an error must be set (not both); errors must include at minimum an error code and message; error codes must be integers. Ask the candidate to state which failure modes or safe-handling strategies are explicitly NOT described by the source. Keep the expected answer concise.
content.suggested_opener: Production logs show responses with non-integer error codes and missing IDs.

content.authoring_prompt: You are designing client-side reconciliation logic that consumes both the upstream MCP Registry and downstream sub-registries. Describe how the client must treat authority, ordering, and freshness when reconciling entries. List concrete implementation measures to avoid connecting to stale, removed, or conflicting server entries. Ensure your design treats the upstream MCP Registry as the primary source of truth and shows how to honor it.
content.suggested_opener: During integration testing, upstream MCP Registry and sub-registries provide conflicting server metadata.

content.authoring_prompt: Given the MCP Registry is the centralized, self-reported starting point, describe operational checks required before using a discovered server in production. List and justify a minimum set of verification steps (verify metadata provenance, apply enterprise allowlist/approval policies, isolate or sandbox unknown/unvetted servers). Explain how these checks integrate with downstream consumers who “massage and deliver to their end-users” and how to enforce them in deployment pipelines. Briefly describe trade-offs and a short rollout plan for vetting existing registry entries.
content.suggested_opener: During onboarding, the MCP Registry lists several self-reported servers needing vetting.

content.authoring_prompt: Describe the operational steps a client must take after the Registry denylist retroactively removes a server. Include immediate actions (what to stop: discovery and connections), updates to local registry/caches, and how to surface the change to operators. Explain any remediation that should be triggered (for example, credential revocation or user notification). Prioritize the steps and note any ordering constraints.
content.suggested_opener: During deployment, a Registry denylist retroactively removes a known server.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze architectural implications of servers expressing intent using abstract modelPreferences (priority values and optional hints). Explain how clients must interpret priorities and map hints — treated as flexible substrings evaluated in order — to models they actually have access to, and how they may map hints to equivalent models from other providers. Discuss design choices for enforcing that clients retain control over actual model access, selection, and permissions, given that hints are advisory and clients make the final model selection. Identify key failure modes and mitigation strategies.
content.suggested_opener: During design, servers send abstract modelPreferences; clients map hints to providers.

content.authoring_prompt: Design an implementable sampling-control subsystem for a client-server AI service. Include a human-in-the-loop that can deny sampling requests and UI flows to review and edit prompts and generated responses. Specify explicit user-approval controls, message validation rules, respect for model preference hints, and rate limiting strategy. Show concrete API endpoints, data schemas, sequence steps, and the structured JSON-RPC error payload for a denial (example: 'User rejected sampling request'). Explain how both parties will handle sensitive data appropriately and where human approval checkpoints occur.
content.suggested_opener: During design, product requires a human-in-the-loop to deny sampling requests.

content.authoring_prompt: Ask candidates to describe how a server should handle failed sampling/createMessage requests according to the spec. Require a concrete JSON-RPC error response example that preserves the request id and includes an error object with a numeric code and human-readable message (use code -1 and message "User rejected sampling request" as the exemplar). Have them explain that clients MUST declare the sampling capability during initialization and that servers must only send sampling requests to clients that advertised it. Finally, require a brief server-side pseudocode sketch showing the server treating JSON-RPC error responses as the canonical failure signal.
content.suggested_opener: A production issue occurs when servers send sampling requests without declared sampling capability.

content.authoring_prompt: Given a system exchanging base64-encoded binary payloads, describe concrete implementation steps to validate the 'data' field and declared 'mimeType'. Specify the user-approval controls and rate limiting/quota controls clients should enforce. Explain how both parties must handle sensitive data, logging, and telemetry to avoid accidental leakage. Include explicit checks for malformed or mismatched binary data and mitigations for abusive/DoS behavior from oversized or frequent payloads.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you find base64-encoded image uploads lacking validation

content.authoring_prompt: Implement the server-side behavior for an SSE stream that responds to JSON-RPC requests sent in a POST. Provide pseudocode or a design sketch that ensures one JSON-RPC response per POSTed request (responses may be batched) and allows the server to send related JSON-RPC requests/notifications before those responses. Show logic that prevents closing the SSE stream until every request has a response (except when a session expires), treats disconnection as not-a-cancel, and supports resumable streams to reduce message loss. Include how the server handles explicit client cancellation via an MCP CancelledNotification and how responses are correlated to requests.
content.suggested_opener: During testing, clients send MCP CancelledNotification to cancel SSE-stream JSON-RPC requests.

content.authoring_prompt: Provide concrete implementation details for a Streamable HTTP server. Show code or configuration pseudocode that validates the Origin header on all incoming connections. Show how to configure the server to bind to localhost (127.0.0.1) instead of 0.0.0.0 when running locally and describe how to implement proper authentication for all connections. Explain how omitting these protections enables DNS rebinding or remote web pages to interact with local MCP/Streamable HTTP servers and the practical consequences.
content.suggested_opener: While testing Streamable HTTP locally, the server accepts any Origin header.

content.authoring_prompt: IMPLEMENTATION: Design the server-side behavior required to implement the quoted protocol rules. Describe how the server ensures each JSON-RPC message is sent on exactly one concurrently connected SSE stream and never broadcast to multiple streams. Specify how SSE event id values are assigned on a per-stream basis, how the server handles an HTTP GET including Last-Event-ID to resume a disconnected stream, and how it decides which messages may be replayed (only those belonging to the disconnected stream). Include brief pseudocode or a short sequence of steps that demonstrates correctness and resumability.
content.suggested_opener: Your service assigns per-stream SSE ids for resumable JSON-RPC delivery.

content.authoring_prompt: Implement the client-side HTTP handling for Mcp-Session-Id in the Streamable HTTP transport. Provide pseudocode or real code showing: accept an Mcp-Session-Id in InitializeResult and include it on all subsequent requests; validate session IDs contain only visible ASCII (0x21–0x7E) and treat them as globally unique/cryptographically secure; on receiving HTTP 404 for a request containing an Mcp-Session-Id, start a new session by sending an InitializeRequest without any session ID; send HTTP DELETE with the Mcp-Session-Id to explicitly terminate a session and handle possible HTTP 405 and HTTP 400 responses. Include short request/response sequences or unit-test cases demonstrating each behavior.
content.suggested_opener: Your team observes HTTP 404 responses to requests containing an Mcp-Session-Id.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain exactly what a receiver MUST do when it receives a tasks/result request for a task in a non-terminal status (for example: working or input_required). Quote or paraphrase the governing requirement, including the definition of terminal status (completed, failed, or cancelled). Finally, explicitly state what the source does not specify about requestor behavior such as polling or interim updates.
content.suggested_opener: During an integration test, a client sends tasks/result while task is working.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze why MCP tasks are requestor-driven and the design tradeoffs that follow. Specify the responsibilities of requestors (augment requests with task metadata; poll for task results) and of receivers (decide which request types support task-based execution; manage task lifecycles). Evaluate the role of capability negotiation — exchanging `tasks` capabilities during initialization — and the implications of the `SHOULD`/`SHOULD NOT` guidance about creating tasks.
content.suggested_opener: During initialization, two services exchange `tasks` capabilities before requests begin.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain how a receiver should enforce task isolation when an authorization context is provided. Provide a concise implementation sketch or pseudocode that shows binding tasks to the authorization context and rejecting tasks/get, tasks/result, and tasks/cancel requests for tasks outside that context. Describe the required fallback when context-binding is unavailable: generating cryptographically secure task IDs with sufficient entropy and using shorter TTL durations to reduce the exposure window. Include one concrete request example and one test case that validates correct rejection.
content.suggested_opener: A production incident occurs when tasks/get returns results across authorization contexts.

content.authoring_prompt: Create an application-style exam question that gives candidates concrete server capability and tool declarations and asks them to determine correct client and server behavior. Include three cases: (A) server capabilities do not include tasks.requests.tools.call; (B) capabilities include tasks.requests.tools.call and execution.taskSupport is absent or "forbidden"; (C) capabilities include tasks.requests.tools.call and execution.taskSupport is "required". For each case, require the candidate to state whether clients may attempt task augmentation, what the server should/must return (including -32601/"Method not found" where appropriate), and cite the MUST/SHOULD normative language. Provide model answers and a 0–5 point grading rubric.
content.suggested_opener: During integration tests, the server advertises tasks.requests.tools.call but execution.taskSupport is absent

content.authoring_prompt: Implement server-side handling for tasks/get, tasks/result, and tasks/cancel per the quoted protocol. Return standard JSON-RPC error -32602 for invalid or nonexistent taskId in those endpoints. Reject tasks/cancel requests for terminal-status tasks (completed, failed, cancelled) with error -32602. For valid cancellation, attempt to stop execution and transition the task to cancelled before responding; ensure cancelled remains even if execution later completes or fails. Describe how your implementation handles deletion and ttl-based purging of cancelled or expired tasks.
content.suggested_opener: An API gateway issues tasks/cancel for a taskId already marked completed.

content.authoring_prompt: You are given a STDIO-based MCP server that currently emits logs to stdout. Modify the implementation so it never writes to standard output—avoid print(), console.log(), fmt.Println(), etc.—keeping stdout reserved exclusively for the MCP JSON-RPC stream. Provide the minimal code changes or clear pseudocode in your chosen language and describe how you would verify that JSON-RPC messages are no longer corrupted. Finally, state when standard output logging is acceptable and why (hint: HTTP-based servers).
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you find print()/console.log()/fmt.Println() in a STDIO-based server

content.authoring_prompt: Design and describe a server-side implementation that ensures Tools can only be executed after explicit user authorization. Provide concrete API endpoints and request/response examples showing how user approval is obtained and checked before a Tool call. Explain how the server records and enforces user approval for subsequent Tool requests and how it handles absent or denied approval. Tie your design to MCP capabilities: Resources, Tools, and Prompts.
content.suggested_opener: A production server receives a Tool call from the LLM without recorded user approval.

content.authoring_prompt: Design a concrete implementation for an MCP client that works over both local (in-process/IPC) and remote (networked) transports. Provide pseudocode or a sequence of actions for explicit connection establishment/handshake, timeout handling, reconnection with backoff, and graceful shutdown for remote transports. Specify how message processing tolerates reordering and duplicates and avoids assuming FIFO or duplicate-free delivery. Call out exactly which lifecycle and reliability assumptions differ between local and remote transports and how your implementation enforces those differences.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you find no connection establishment/handshake for remote transport

content.authoring_prompt: Describe what will break if SDKs do not enforce protocol compliance with type safety across local and remote transport protocols. Specify concrete design requirements for serialization, prompts, and callbacks to adhere strictly to the shared protocol and its type contracts. Explain how each SDK and transport can validate and handle data consistently. Keep responses focused on protocol compliance and type safety.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review you find serialization ignores protocol compliance with type safety

content.authoring_prompt: Describe realistic interoperability failures that occur when SDKs or spec versions diverge in functionality or protocol features. Explain how ensuring all SDKs provide the same core functionality and full protocol support, and building MCP clients that can connect to any MCP server, prevents and recovers from those failures. Give concrete examples of cross-SDK mismatches and show how alignment of implementations reduces them.
content.suggested_opener: During a production incident, MCP clients fail due to SDK protocol mismatches.

content.authoring_prompt: Design and document a client implementation that keeps its cached view of available tools correct when the server declares the tools capability with "listChanged": true. Treat notifications/notifications/tools/list_changed as a hint, not as authoritative. Specify explicit discovery or polling and fallbacks such as periodic or manual refresh. Provide concise pseudo-code or algorithmic steps showing how the client re-checks the server's authoritative tool list and updates its cache.
content.suggested_opener: Server declared tools capability with listChanged true but emits few notifications.

content.authoring_prompt: You have a server exposing the Tools API but client discovery and notifications are failing. Ask the candidate to (a) explain why a server MUST declare the tools capability in its capabilities document, (b) provide the exact JSON snippet that declares tools with listChanged set to true, and (c) describe the operational problems that occur when the tools capability is omitted (clients unaware of tools or listChanged, missed or stale tool information).
content.suggested_opener: During a deployment, clients stop receiving listChanged notifications for tools.

content.authoring_prompt: You're designing a client UI for an application where an LLM may invoke tools. List concrete client-side controls and UI elements that implement the spec: make clear which tools are exposed to the AI model, insert visual indicators when tools are invoked, present confirmation prompts (with extra prompts for sensitive actions), show tool inputs before calling the server, validate tool results before passing them to the LLM, implement timeouts for tool calls, and log tool usage for audit. For each control, describe the user flow, the UI element shown, and how an operator can deny or review the invocation.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you notice AI tools exposed without confirmation prompts.

content.authoring_prompt: Write a brief implementation plan and concise pseudocode for an MCP client that treats the set of tools as dynamic. The client must call tools/list on demand and subscribe to notifications/tools/list_changed to learn about additions, removals, or updates at runtime. Show the exact call sequence you perform immediately before invoking any tool and how list_changed notifications update the client's authoritative view. In one short paragraph, explain how using on-demand listing together with list_changed prevents race conditions.
content.suggested_opener: A production agent must call tools/list and subscribe to notifications/tools/list_changed.

content.authoring_prompt: Write code or clear pseudocode that produces a tool result object representing a runtime error. Set isError to true and place human-readable error details inside the result's content array. Explain briefly why escalating tool errors as MCP protocol-level errors prevents the LLM from observing or handling them. Describe how the LLM could use the content array to decide remediation, retries, or human-in-the-loop actions.
content.suggested_opener: During testing, a tool emits a runtime error but escalates it to MCP protocol-level.

content.authoring_prompt: Implement a function that disambiguates tool names when aggregating tools from multiple MCP servers. The function should accept the tool name plus server metadata (user-defined server name and server URI) and return a unique tool identifier using one of the safe strategies: concatenating a user-defined server name, generating a random prefix, or using the server URI as a prefix. Do not rely on the initialization-provided name for uniqueness. Provide brief tests demonstrating each strategy and a 2-3 sentence rationale comparing their trade-offs.
content.suggested_opener: During integration, MCP servers expose tools with identical initialization-provided names.

content.authoring_prompt: Design and implement a UI approval gate that enforces explicit human-in-the-loop approval before any model-invoked tool executes. Define an audit log schema and retention policy that records approvals, invocations, denials, and related metadata for traceability. Provide API contracts and server-side invocation code that require approval tokens and never surface internal errors or diagnostics to clients. Include brief UI mockups, access-control rules, and example sanitization/error-handling snippets.
content.suggested_opener: During an integration, model-controlled tools require human-in-the-loop approval in UI.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze the architectural tradeoffs between representing a resource with an https:// URI versus using another or a custom URI scheme and serving the resource contents through MCP. Explain the conditions under which servers SHOULD use https:// per the quoted guidance and when they SHOULD prefer another scheme. Describe the practical implementation implications: which party performs fetching and when the server must download or proxy contents via MCP. Keep the explanation concise and grounded in the provided guidance.
content.suggested_opener: An engineer asks whether to publish resources as https:// URIs or via MCP.

content.authoring_prompt: Provide implementation-level pseudocode or code snippets enforcing the documented security requirements. Validate all resource URIs (including file:// mappings) before any operation; properly encode binary data when returning contents (for example, base64 in a blob field); and perform permission checks before listing or returning contents. Show how to implement access controls for sensitive resources and include a resource annotation example with an audience array containing the valid values "user" and "assistant". For each MUST/SHOULD, add a one-line justification of where and why it is enforced.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review, you find file:// mappings exposed without URI validation.

content.authoring_prompt: Analyze the provided spec excerpt about resourceTemplates and the completion API. Identify what the excerpt explicitly states and which claims in the candidate answer are inferred rather than quoted. For each inferred recommendation (for example, “clients must expand templates themselves”), explain whether the excerpt justifies it and list alternative client behaviors that remain consistent with the spec. Support every conclusion by citing exact phrases or lines from the excerpt.
content.suggested_opener: A CI job logs a resources/templates/list response containing uriTemplate file:///{path}.

content.authoring_prompt: Require the candidate to implement server-side handling for a resources/read request that fails. They must show when to return JSON-RPC error -32002 versus -32603, and produce an error object with code -32002, a human-readable message (for example "Resource not found") and structured error.data containing the requested uri. Include the mandatory resource URI validation step and provide minimal pseudocode plus example JSON-RPC responses for both failure paths.
content.suggested_opener: A client issues a resources/read request for an unvalidated resource URI.

content.authoring_prompt: Provide examinees the quoted line: “Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications…”. Then present a student response that asserts specific protocol mechanics as requirements. Ask candidates to analyze whether the quoted text supports those specific mechanics, identifying each unsupported claim and explaining why. Require a concise model answer and a short rubric that grants full credit only if the respondent concludes the quote is a high-level analogy and cannot by itself justify the listed mechanics.
content.suggested_opener: Your team treats MCP like USB-C when connecting AI applications to systems.

content.authoring_prompt: Refer to the guidance: "Create MCP servers to expose your data and tools." Analyze why keeping the server role (exposing data and tools) distinct from the client role (consuming resources and orchestrating them) is recommended. Describe architectural tradeoffs and concrete implementation problems that arise if those roles are collapsed into a monolith, emphasizing the loss of the operational boundary between exposing resources and consuming/orchestrating them. Conclude with a prioritized list of the top three impacts.
content.suggested_opener: During a design review, MCP servers are being merged into a single monolith.

content.authoring_prompt: Explain why a client API exposes explicit capability flags that are set at construction time, as shown by ClientCapabilities.builder().roots(true).sampling().elicitation(). For each capability—filesystem roots support (with list-change notifications), LLM sampling support, and elicitation capability—analyze plausible implementation trade-offs and operational implications of enabling them. Base your analysis only on the concepts shown in the snippet and give concise, engineer-focused guidance for a design decision.
content.suggested_opener: Your team must decide whether to enable roots, sampling, and elicitation.

content.authoring_prompt: You are reviewing a transport configured with a custom HttpRequest.Builder that embeds a never-expiring token. Describe the security and operational risks of using a static HttpRequest.Builder and explain why it prevents per-request credential rotation. When dynamic authentication is needed, state the correct approach and name the interfaces to implement. Briefly explain at a high level how implementing McpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer or McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer lets the transport adjust authentication at request time.
content.suggested_opener: A production incident shows transport always sends the same never-expiring token.

content.authoring_prompt: Using the roots capability, describe what breaks when client.addRoot or client.removeRoot is invoked without client.rootsListChangedNotification. Explain how the server's view of accessible filesystem roots becomes stale and why that can lead to incorrect or unsafe behavior. Give two concrete examples of failures or safety issues that could result and state the correct client-side notification sequence.
content.suggested_opener: During testing, addRoot and removeRoot calls occur without notification.

content.authoring_prompt: Describe the failure mode when the wrong HTTP request customizer type is registered for an MCP transport. Be explicit which interfaces the transport expects: McpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer or McpAsyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer, and explain why the customizer type must match the MCP client type. State the resulting observable behavior on HTTP request modifications.
content.suggested_opener: During a code review you spot McpSyncHttpClientRequestCustomizer used with async MCP client

content.authoring_prompt: Write a short implementation that ensures the client initializes the connection before calling any APIs. For a sync client show McpClient.sync(transport).build(); call client.initialize(); then call client.listTools(). For an async client describe the async initialize flow you would follow. In 2–4 sentences explain why initialize() is required (mention MCP session, protocol and capability negotiation, and change/notification consumers) and what may fail if it is skipped.
content.suggested_opener: During deployment, the McpSyncClient fails to call initialize() before listTools().
